stem:
An 8 year old child presents with vomiting, stridor, difficulty breathing and poor perfusion after eating a chocolate bar given to him by a friend. His heart rate is 160 bpm with a weak, thready pulse. His respiratory rate is 40 per minute, oxygen saturations 95% in room air and blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg. He is pale and sweaty and is struggling to keep his eyes open when you ask him questions.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate chest x-ray to rule out foreign body
Try to calm him down and then re-assess his vital signs

explanation: This child has anaphylaxis with airway involvement (stridor), respiratory symptoms, and shock (hypotension, poor perfusion) after a likely food trigger. The most appropriate immediate treatment is intramuscular adrenaline. Oxygen is supportive but must not delay adrenaline.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Breathing difficulties

rationale: Preserved existing options because one option was clearly the single best answer.

optionExplanations.A: A chest x-ray is not the immediate priority in suspected anaphylaxis and would delay life-saving treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Oxygen may be given as an adjunct, but adrenaline is the key first-line treatment in anaphylaxis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: intramuscular adrenaline is first-line for anaphylaxis, especially with airway symptoms and shock.
optionExplanations.D: Observation without immediate treatment is unsafe in a child with suspected anaphylaxis and haemodynamic compromise.
optionExplanations.E: Penicillin is not indicated; the presentation is most consistent with an allergic reaction/anaphylaxis rather than bacterial infection.
